lines.narration: A sealed bag of pencils and erasers. Lynn gives her name, says the phone is not hers, offers her grades as proof.
In the dark an answer sheet fills itself in, row by row, until a name settles under the bubbles.
Then a file with her name on it. Certificates, a clipping, the record that makes her worth recruiting.
Lynn and her father sit before the administrator, trophies on the desk, a clipping naming her a national crossword champion.
Her father talks the record down to swimming, pushing trophies across. The director stops him - does Lynn want to come?
She answers for herself: the old school suits her better, and a year here costs almost a hundred and fifty thousand.
Sixty thousand a term, two terms. The number arrives handwritten beside her head: 120,000. She keeps itemising.
Her father's hand settles over hers as she finishes the sum - fares, lunch at thirty-five instead of twenty. Not worth it.
Then the figures vanish and the offer lands: what if she studies for free? Her father grins beside the trophies.
An enrolment form for 2557, and a nickname going onto the dotted line.
M.4. Three years gone, and the new school arrives as a queue of white uniforms climbing stone steps.
A stranger starts smoothing Lynn's hair at the backdrop. Three years here, she says, you have to look good. She is Grace.
Alone at a dark table, Grace repeats what people say about them: Lynn is clever, and Grace is stupid.
They spread a maths paper between them. A inside B, intersect C - Lynn walks it while Grace stares at the page.
A hand lands on Lynn's shoulder. Teach me how - and the astonishment is at Lynn, not the maths.
Grace names the terms: homework every evening, and she will be the first student Lynn ever teaches.
Back at the bare table: she only helped a friend study. She taught her nothing wrong. Did she?
Midterm. A hall of white uniforms, and Lynn at her desk with her head already down, writing.
Two seats over, Grace's page is blank - then a Venn diagram she knows, the same question off Lynn's pink worksheet.
Grace twists round and whispers back. Lynn answers alert, then her face folds. She knows what is being asked.
The proctor slouches and stifles a yawn. Lynn is the only head in the hall that comes up.
A metal pen, then something small in her fingers: answer letters pencilled down the side of a white eraser.
Lynn checks the front of the room. Grace's head snaps up, expectant. Lynn stays turned away.
She works her foot out of her shoe and drops the eraser inside. Then their eyes meet across the aisle.
The shoe is kicked out. It skids over the tiles and stops upright in the open, answers inside.
A student stands at the invigilator's desk. Under the rows a hand reaches into the shoe for the eraser.
Grace grins down at her sheet and writes. Lynn hands her paper in. Grace sits back with a lollipop.
In the corridor Grace hugs a report book and names the next thing: Pat's place. You have a swimsuit, right?
A robe stitched Patton Hotel Bangkok. Then night, a lit rooftop pool, and a boy surging through the spray: Pat.
Grace surfaces into it: smart people do not understand her, and stupid people still want a good grade.
Pat slaps water into the air and names a price: three thousand baht a term. Lynn lifts her head.
Three thousand each, he says, and five more of them want in. On a dark street, Lynn is still listening.
Thirteen exams, he totals it: two hundred and thirty-four thousand baht. Worth more, he says, than her cleverness.
At home, in the dark, she eases open her father's desk drawer and lifts out a sealed official document.
Under the lamp she sorts the papers and reads. The development fee was paid anyway - 120,000, scholarship or not.
Why this school, she asks from the piano. For chances he never had, he says. He is not like her mother.
He tips a pill into his hand and swallows it. Lynn drops her eyes. He sets the bottle down, smiling.
Alone, she works the same four fingerings until they stop being music. Four shapes, four answers on a multiple-choice sheet.
Paying a friend to teach you music, she will say later, is not illegal in any country.
In the music room she gives six students four chords and a right-hand position to read off her hands.
Three answers right, one wrong, repeated - and hold the scores down so nobody notices. The students stare back blank.
Final exam, 2/2557, half past eight to half past ten. Grace chews her pencil and waits for a hand.
Lynn plays the exam from her own living room while boy after boy reads the tapping hand and inks another row.
A bank book opens on deposits climbing into the hundreds of thousands. Then the house after dark, her father waiting.
On the school tower a banner unrolls: a portrait, congratulations on a scholarship. The school hangs up what it was handed.
